USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The US should proceed with the planned tariff escalation on the remaining ~$300 billion of Chinese goods and maintain pressure on the $200 billion tranche increase to 25%. This is the moment to demonstrate resolve while China's economy is under strain and domestic political support for toughness on China remains strong. Continue negotiations but from a position of demonstrated leverage.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.35 reflects a moderate but not existential threat to US interests. The $419 billion trade deficit with China remains large (BBC, 2019-05-08), and China's structural practices — forced technology transfer, IP theft, state subsidies, and market access restrictions — pose a genuine long-term threat to US tech leadership and competitiveness (USC Annenberg analysis; Fox Business). However, the US economy is performing well (Dow up ~11% YTD in 2019 per BBC), giving Washington room to absorb short-term costs. The action score of -1.0 (maximal escalation via tariffs) is justified because: (1) China has been backsliding on commitments during negotiations, as reported when talks collapsed in May 2019 (BBC: 'claims Beijing is trying to row back on a trade deal'); (2) Senator Graham and others frame this as a once-in-a-generation opportunity to change China's 'cheating ways' (Fox Business, 2019-05-12); (3) White House adviser Kudlow acknowledged 'both sides will pay' but the structural leverage favors the US since China's export-dependent economy is more vulnerable to supply chain disruption (Fox Business); (4) China's retaliation has been limited to $110 billion vs. US tariffs on $250 billion, indicating asymmetric leverage. The risk of escalation is real — IMF has cut global growth forecasts citing trade tensions (BBC) — but the cost of acquiescence to the status quo is higher, as it would entrench China's state-led model in the industries of the future (AI, cloud, robotics, green tech per USC analysis).
key_factors: $419 billion US trade deficit with China provides ongoing economic justification for pressure
China reportedly backsliding on trade deal commitments in May 2019 negotiations
US economy strong enough to absorb short-term tariff costs (Dow up 11% YTD)
China's retaliation asymmetrically limited ($110B vs $250B), indicating US leverage advantage
Structural issues (IP theft, forced tech transfer, state subsidies) threaten long-term US tech leadership
IMF cut global growth forecasts citing trade tensions — risk exists but cost of inaction is higher
Domestic political support for China toughness bipartisan (Graham, Fox Business commentary)
China's supply chain dependency creates structural vulnerability to sustained tariff pressure
